## The question

[Matrix multiplication seen as derivative or integral](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4677061/matrix-multiplication-seen-as-derivative-or-integral), asked by [John HHU](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/850906/john-hhu) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-04-11; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I'm reading the book "Introduction to Linear Algebra 5th edition" page 24 about Inverse Matrix, below is the background info. 
>
> $$\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
> \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
> \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3 \end{bmatrix}.$$
>
> In which the author mentioned 
> "The differences $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ become the derivative $\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = b(t)$. In the inverse direction, the sums $\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ become the integral of $b(t)$."
>
> I'm so confused about these statements, I'm thinking he meant vector $\mathbf{x}$ as a function, which applied to matrix $\mathbf{A}$, so $\mathbf{x}(t)$ is the $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$.  Then how could: "$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ become the derivative $\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = b(t)$"? As I cant imagine the derivative of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ or $x(t)$ here.  
>
> $$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 - x_1 \\ x_3 - x_2 \end{bmatrix}$$
>
> * * *
>
> ![book page][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: k73kt.png
:::

A couple of things which help anyone learning linear algebra from Gil Strang's texts:

1. Strang writes in a pretty conversational style, and fills in details after motivating the ideas.
2. Strang's lectures are online and form a good companion to the text.

One remark which might add some context to the portion you clipped comes on page 27:

> This section is looking ahead to key ideas, not fully explained yet.

*What I think* Strang is saying here with “The differences $Ax$ become the derivative $dx/dt$...” etc., is that

* Differential equations $x'(t) = b(t)$ are an infinite-dimensional version of linear equations $Ax=b$.
* If a vector is treated like a time series, the difference matrix $A$ has a lot of the same features of a derivative operator on differentiable functions, and the sum matrix $A^{-1}$ as a lot of the same features as an integration operator.
